# PART 2 – Persistence within countries {#part-2-persistence .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part two takes the problem of the first session, few clusters of unequal weight, and asks what a Bayesian model does about it. The CR2 test repairs the standard errors after the fit. A Bayesian model has no such repair: the dependence of the years of a country has to be written into the model, and a posterior predictive check tells us whether it has been. The model of the first part fails that check. The part ends with a model whose errors persist from year to year, and with your second run, which fits the frequentist twin of that model.
:::

## The dependence of the years {#the-dependence-of-the-years .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: d3-persistence-check
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
# The posterior predictive check of persistence: the correlation within
# countries between the residual of a country-year and that of the year
# before, in 1,000 datasets replicated from each of the four two-way models,
# against its value in the data (companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel_ppc_draws.csv)
bayes_ppc_draws |>
  datawizard::data_modify(model = factor(model, levels = c("common", "slopes", "ar1", "both"),
                                         labels = c("one slope", "a slope for each country", "persistent errors",
                                                    "country slopes and persistence"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(persistence)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, fill = ncl_blue, alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = persistence$observed[1], colour = d_red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(model), ncol = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "correlation of a residual with that of the year before", y = "replicated datasets") +
  theme_slide(12) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 11))
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
- "If the model fits, then replicated data generated under the model should look similar to observed data" [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, p. 143]
- The statistic: the persistence of the residuals, `r fmt_num(persistence$observed[1], 2)` in the data (red line)
- With one slope, the replicated persistence has a median of `r fmt_num(persistence$rep_median[persistence$model == "common"], 2)`, and no replicated dataset reaches the observed value
- The two models with persistent errors pass
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
A model that passes its computational checks may still fail to describe the data. The test is to let the fitted model generate new datasets and compare them with the real one on a statistic that matters, and Bayesian Data Analysis states the principle: replicated data should look like the observed data. The statistic here is the persistence of the residuals, the correlation of the first session, about a half in the data. Look at the top left. The model with one slope replicates a persistence near zero, slightly negative, and not one of its datasets reaches the observed value, because a model with independent errors cannot produce a country that stays above the expected value year after year. Only the two models in the bottom row, in which the errors persist from year to year, reproduce the persistence in the data. The two panels with a slope for each country belong to the third part, and we come back to them there.
:::

## Persistent errors {#persistent-errors .smaller}

$$ e_{ct} = \phi\, e_{c,t-1} + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ct} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) $$

::: {.small}
- The error of each year carries a fraction φ of the error of the year before, `ar(time = year, gr = cntry, p = 1, cov = TRUE)` in brms, under the prior normal(0, 0.5), which is centred on no persistence
- φ has a posterior median of `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$median, 2)` (95% credible interval `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$q2.5, 2)` to `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$q97.5, 2)`), and `r fmt_pct(persistence$p_ppc[persistence$model == "ar1"], 0)` of the replicated values of persistence lie above the observed one
- The slope moves and widens, to a median of `r fmt_num(ar1$median, 5)` (95% credible interval `r fmt_num(ar1$q2.5, 5)` to `r fmt_num(ar1$q97.5, 5)`): the likelihood compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from the change from one year to the next
:::

::: notes
The failed check names the next model. Let the error of each year carry a fraction phi of the error of the year before, a first-order autoregressive process within each country, with a prior on phi centred on no persistence. The posterior puts phi at about three quarters, and the model passes the check. The slope moves as well as widening, because the likelihood now compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from changes from one year to the next than from the level of a year against the decade mean of its country.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – Persistence held fixed {#hands-on-2-persistence-held-fixed .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, in the console:

1. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice:

   ```{.r}
   euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
   fit <- nlme::gls(mcosmo ~ unemp + cntry + factor(year), data = euframes,
                    correlation = nlme::corAR1(0.5, form = ~ year | cntry, fixed = TRUE))
   summary(fit)$tTable["unemp", ]
   ```
2. Run it with 0, 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95 in place of 0.5, and note the slope and its standard error each time. At 0 the fit is the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification
3. **Which of these comparisons is the claim about, and what does the posterior of φ say about the choice between them?** Two sentences for your notes
:::

::: notes
The frequentist twin of the model with persistent errors runs in a second, so you can do by hand what the posterior does by averaging. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice, and note the slope and its standard error. At nought you get the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification. As you raise the value towards one, the comparison shifts from the level of each year against the decade mean of its country towards the change from one year to the next, and the slope moves towards zero while its standard error grows. Then write two sentences: which of these comparisons is the claim, as the paper states it, about, and what does the posterior of phi, about three quarters, say about the choice between them? [state the time]
:::
